value.overview: The Gartered Violaceous Trogon, also called the Gartered Trogon, is a colorful forest bird of the trogon family. It occurs from southern Mexico through Central America to western Ecuador and parts of northwestern South America. Males have violet-blue and green upperparts, a dark face, a yellow eye-ring, and yellow underparts. Females are mainly gray with a pale eye-ring. It usually watches from a quiet perch before flying out to capture prey or take fruit.
value.classification: The Gartered Violaceous Trogon is Trogon caligatus in the family Trogonidae, which includes trogons and quetzals. It belongs to the order Trogoniformes.
value.identification: This medium-sized trogon is about 23–25 cm long and has the broad body, short legs, and long tail typical of the group. The male has a dark head and face, violet-blue throat and upper breast, green to bluish back, yellow belly, and a conspicuous yellow ring around the eye. The female is mostly gray above and below, with a pale whitish eye-ring and less strongly marked tail barring. In Costa Rica, the yellow eye-ring is a particularly useful field mark.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from tropical Mexico through Central America to western Ecuador and parts of northwestern Amazonia. In Costa Rica it is a widespread lowland and foothill resident, occurring on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, including the Area de Conservación Guanacaste. It uses humid and semi-humid forest, forest edges, second growth, wooded clearings, and parts of seasonally dry forest. It is most often seen in the middle and upper levels or canopy, and in Costa Rica may occur up to about 1,200 meters.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica and is not known for regular long-distance migration. Individuals may make local movements in response to food availability, rainfall, or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding activity has been reported mainly from February through June. The species nests in a cavity in a tree, often where decay has created a suitable chamber. Both members of a pair participate in territory defense and care of the nest. The nest site is usually placed above the ground in wooded habitat, and the young remain dependent on the adults after leaving the cavity. Details of nesting behavior can vary across its broad range.
value.dietFeeding: The Gartered Violaceous Trogon feeds mainly on insects and other large arthropods, including caterpillars, grasshoppers, katydids, phasmids, and ants. It also eats fruits from a variety of trees and shrubs, including Cecropia in Costa Rica. A bird commonly sits motionless on an exposed branch, scans nearby foliage, and then makes a short flight to seize prey before returning to a perch or moving to another lookout.
value.behavior: This trogon is usually quiet and unobtrusive despite its bright plumage. It spends much of its time perched in the middle levels or canopy, often remaining still for long periods. Foraging flights are generally short and direct. It may occur alone, in pairs, or occasionally near mixed-species feeding groups. Its rounded wings and relatively weak-looking flight are typical of trogons, which rely more on patient ambushes than on prolonged aerial pursuit.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is not precisely quantified, but the species remains broadly distributed and locally common in suitable habitat.
